abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: The current highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART or ART) effectively suppresses de novo HIV‐1 infection but fails to eliminate HIV reservoir cells, which leads to rapid viral rebound upon ART cessation. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells engineered to target HIV‐1 Env⁺ cells offer a promising strategy to eliminate or control these persistent reservoirs and achieve durable control of HIV‐1 infection. However, a major challenge is the susceptibility of such CAR‐T cells to HIV infection, especially those soluble CD4 (sCD4)‐based CAR‐T cells. In this study, an sCD4‐based CAR incorporating the S85C mutation in the CD4 Ig‐like domain 1 (termed D1C) was engineered to enable disulfide bond formation with the HIV‐1 envelope glycoprotein (Env), thereby reducing viral entry and conferring protection against HIV infection. D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells exhibited enhanced T‐cell activation and cytotoxicity in response to Env stimulation while demonstrating resistance HIV‐1 infection in vitro and in vivo. Furthermore, the herpesvirus entry mediator (HVEM) intracellular domain was identified as an optimal costimulatory domain, enhancing cytokine induction, cytotoxicity, and promoting a favorable central memory phenotype and persistence of CAR‐T cells. In humanized mouse models, D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells demonstrated superior persistence and improved control of HIV rebound following ART interruption compared to wild‐type (WT)/sCD4 CAR‐T cells. These findings highlight a novel strategy to enhance the efficacy and durability of HIV‐targeted CAR‐T cell therapy by combining HIV resistance and optimized co‐stimulation.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Immunotherapy, particularly chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy, has emerged as a promising strategy for controlling HIV infection [1, 2, 3, 4]. Unlike traditional antiretroviral therapy (ART), which suppresses viral replication but does not eradicate latent reservoirs, CAR‐T cells engineered to recognize and eliminate HIV‐infected cells offer a novel approach to achieving sustained viral remission [5, 6, 7]. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that CAR T cells can effectively suppress HIV‐1 replication and eliminate HIV‐1‐expressing cells in vitro and in animal models [8, 9], leading to the initiation of early‐phase clinical trials to evaluate their safety and efficacy in humans [3, 10].

A key target for anti‐HIV strategies is the HIV envelope glycoprotein (Env), which facilitates viral entry into host cells. Single‐chain variable fragments (scFvs) derived from broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) have been incorporated into CAR T cell constructs, enabling precise targeting and elimination of HIV‐infected cells expressing the Env on their surface [10]. The other targeting strategy of the anti‐HIV CAR‐T cells relies on soluble CD4 (sCD4)‐based domains that interact with the viral envelope [8]. Nevertheless, critical challenges persist, including optimal antigen targeting and the susceptibility of infused CAR T cell products to HIV infection [11, 12, 13]. Especially, sCD4‐based CARs are susceptible to HIV infection due to CD4 serving as the natural ligand for the gp120 envelope protein of HIV. As the main target of HIV, infused CD4+ CAR T cells, attracted to an HIV‐infected cell risk becoming infected, thus limiting their therapeutic benefit [9, 14].

It has been reported that a specific mutation, S85C, in the extracellular immunoglobulin (Ig) domain 1 of CD4 can form a disulfide bond with HIV‐1 Env126C [15]. This structural modification prevents HIV‐1 fusion and entry, providing a potential mechanism for enhancing resistance. Incorporation of the S85C mutation into the CD4 extracellular Ig domain of CAR T cells was hypothesized to confer resistance to HIV infection while promoting covalent interaction between sCD4 and HIV‐1 Env, thereby improving the efficacy and durability of CAR T therapy for HIV treatment. By integrating this mutation, the study aimed to address the critical challenge of Env‐targeting CAR T cell susceptibility to HIV‐1 infection, potentially leading to more effective and durable therapeutic outcomes. This study explored the application of S85C‐mutated CD4 CAR T cells in HIV therapy, evaluated their ability to resist HIV infection while maintaining or enhancing their functions to eliminate HIV Env+ target cells.

sec.title: sCD4/CAR With S85C Mutation Within the Ig‐Like Domain 1 (D1C) Confers Resistance to HIV Infection
sec.p: To overcome the limitation that HIV Env‐targeting CAR on T cells also serve as receptors for HIV infection, the S85C mutation was introduced within the Ig‐like domain 1 of CD4, enabling disulfide bond formation with HIV Env upon CD4 binding [15]. The constructs were evaluated in 293 T cells expressing different sCD4‐based CAR designs: sCD4 containing the full‐length extracellular domain (D1–D4) (FL/sCD4), Wild Type sCD4 comprising Domain 1 and Domain 2 (WT/sCD4), sCD4 Domain 1 and Domain 2 with the S85C mutation (D1C/sCD4), and sCD4 Domain 1 and Domain 2 with both S85C and A80F mutations (D1FC/sCD4). The A80F mutation leads to loss of CD4 binding with HIV Env [16]. These engineered sCD4 variants served as the extracellular antigen‐binding components targeting the CD4‐binding site of HIV Env in CAR‐T constructs. As illustrated in Figure 1A, all CAR constructs, except for FL/sCD4, included the costimulatory domain (CSD) 4‐1BB and the TCR CD3ζ (ζ) chain, with the CD8 transmembrane (TM) domain. These HIV Env‐specific CARs were expressed on the 293 T cell surface at similar levels as detected by anti‐CD4 mAb or the c‐myc tag.

Created with BioRender. (B) Diagram of D1C‐mediated resistance to HIV infection and of the HIV luciferase reporter assay. Created with BioRender. (C) Engineered 293T cells and (D) transduced primary human CD8⁺ T cells were infected with serial dilutions of HIV Env–pseudotyped HIV‐1 luciferase (HIV‐Luc) virus. P‐values calculated using ordinary two‐way ANOVA Turkeys multiple comparisons test. *p < 0.05. **p < 0.01. ***p < 0.001.

sec.p: The capacity of each sCD4 variant to support HIV‐1 infection was assessed using an HIV luciferase reporter virus pseudotyped with HIV‐1 R3A Env (Figure 1B). 293 T cells transfected with sCD4‐based CARs were infected with varying doses of the NL4‐Luc/R3A virus. As expected, 293 T cells expressing full‐length CD4 extracellular domain (293 FL/sCD4) were most susceptible to HIV infection, and CD4 wild‐type D1D2‐derived CAR construct supported 10‐fold lower level of HIV‐1 infection. The D1C/sCD4 CAR demonstrated a significantly lower infection rate compared to WT/sCD4 CAR (Figure 1C). The D1FC/sCD4 CAR showed complete resistance to HIV infection, as the A80F mutation disrupted the binding between CD4 and the HIV Env [16]. There was no difference in supporting vesicular stomatitis virus glycoprotein (VSV‐G) pseudotyped HIV‐Luciferase virus infection in those 293 T cells expressing various sCD4 constructs (Figure S1A).

When tested in human primary T cells, CD8+ CAR‐T cells expressing WT/sCD4 supported HIV‐1 infection, and the D1C/sCD4 CAR T cells were significantly protected from HIV infection (Figure 1D). The low level of infection was probably due to contaminating CD4 T cells, as GFP vector‐transduced cells also supported the low level of HIV infection (Figure 1D). There was no difference in VSV‐G mediated infection in CD8+ T cells expressing various sCD4 CARs (Figure 1E). Furthermore, CD4+ CAR‐T cells expressing the D1C/sCD4 CAR were also partially protected from HIV infection (Figure S1B), suggesting interference of D1C/sCD4 CAR with the endogenous CD4 receptor. These findings confirm that introducing the S85C mutation into the CD4 Domain 1 α‐helix, which forms an intermolecular disulfide bond between CD4 and Env and blocks Env intramolecular disulfide bond upon CD4 binding, can inhibit HIV‐1 fusion and entry [15]. Therefore, D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells with the S85C mutation are resistant to HIV‐1 infection.

sec.title: HVEM‐Based CAR‐T Cells With D1C (S85C) Mutation Have Stronger Functions Via Env‐Binding Mechanism
sec.p: Given prior observations that the herpesvirus entry mediator (HVEM) derived CSD augments CAR‐T effector function relative to 4‐1BB or CD28 CSD [17, 18], HVEM‐based D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells were evaluated against K562 cells engineered to express HIV‐1 Env(K.Env) (Figure 2A–C). Under identical lentiviral transduction conditions multiplicity of infection (MOI), WT/sCD4 and D1C/sCD4 CAR T cells expressed similar levels of CAR surface expression. These two CAR designs elicited strong interleukin‐2 (IL‐2) and interferon‐gamma (IFN‐γ) responses, whereas nontransduced T cells, GFP controls, and the D1FC/sCD4 variant showed no induction of cytokines (Figure 2B). Notably, D1C CAR‐T cells produced significantly more IL‐2 than WT/sCD4 CAR‐T cells, while both exhibited comparable levels of IFN‐γ secretion (Figure 2B). To evaluate cytotoxic function, CD8⁺ CAR‐T cells were co‐cultured with K.Env target cells at varying effector‐to‐target (E:T) ratios. After coculture, both D1C‐HM and wild‐type herpes virus entry mediator (HVEM) mutant (WT‐HM) CAR‐T cells exhibited robust, dose‐dependent cytotoxicity compared to control groups. Importantly, D1C‐HM CAR‐T cells exhibited significantly greater cytolytic activity than WT‐HM CAR‐T cells across multiple E:T ratios (Figure 2C). In independent stimulation assays, D1C‐HM CAR‐T cells also secreted higher IL‐2 levels when exposed to recombinant gp140 [19, 20], a trimeric Env protein, compared to WT‐HM CAR‐T cells (Figure 2D). Similar results were observed with 4‐1BB‐based D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells on cytokine production (Figure S2A–D), suggesting that the D1C/sCD4 CAR influences T cell activation and effector function in response to HIV‐Env stimulation. Neither D1C‐HM nor WT‐HM CAR‐T cells were activated by Env− K562 (Figure S2E), confirming their Env‐dependent activity.

(B, C) Different CAR‐T cells were cocultured with HIV‐1 Env+ target cells. (B) Summary of IL‐2 and IFN‐γ production at Day 3 after co‐culture of CAR‐T cells with K562‐Env at E/T ratio of 1 to 10 (n = 3). (C) Summary of frequency of HIVYU2 Envelope+ K562 cells (K.Env) at D3 after coculture with human‐derived CAR‐T cells and nontransduced (NT) T cells at different E/T ratios. (D) Summary of IL‐2 and IFN‐γ production from co‐culture assays, in which 5 × 10⁵ CAR‐T cells were independently stimulated for 24 h with 4 µg recombinant gp140 protein. (E) CAR‐Jurkats were seeded with K562 cells or K562‐Env+ on the cell surface at a density of 3 × 105 at different target‐to‐effector ratios. Trogocytosis (%CAR + PKH26 +) was determined by fluorescence‐activated cell sorting (FACS) 6‐h post commencement of co‐culture. One‐way or two‐way ANOVA, with Tukey's multiple comparisons test, was applied as appropriate for each dataset. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001. Statistical comparisons in Figure C were performed between the D1C‐HM group and each of the following groups individually: D1FC‐HM and WT‐HM, at indicated E/T ratios.

sec.p: Trogocytosis is the transfer of membrane and surface proteins from target cells to CAR‐T cells during contact [21]. To test if the D1C mutation affects trogocytosis with altered covalent antigen‐binding affinity, a trogocytosis assay was conducted. The results showed that the D1C (S85C) mutant did not increase or otherwise alter trogocytosis in CD4‐based CAR‐T cells despite enhanced functional activity (Figure 2E, S2F–H). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells, while resistant to HIV‐1 infection, showed elevated cytokine secretion and cytotoxic capabilities against HIV‐1 Env⁺ target cells with comparable levels of trogocytosis as WT/sCD4 CAR‐T cells.

sec.title: HVEM CSD‐Derived CAR T Cells Display Superior Effector Functions Associated With T cm Phenotype
sec.p: To confirm that HVEM‐based D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells possess superior anti‐HIV activity over CD28‐ or 41BB‐based CAR T cells (Figure 3A), D1C/sCD4 CAR constructs with their respective CSDs were tested in primary human CD8⁺ T cells. Flow cytometric analysis 5 days posttransduction confirmed efficient expression of all constructs in CD8⁺ T cells, based on staining with anti‐CD8 and anti‐Myc antibodies. No significant differences were observed in cell viability or expansion among CAR‐T cells with different CSDs (Figure S3A). The maturation phenotype of D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells bearing different CSDs was next characterized. After 12 days of culture, memory T cell subsets were assessed via surface expression of CD45RO and CCR7. While nontransduced control CD8⁺ T cells primarily exhibited a terminal effector (Tte) phenotype, all CAR‐T cells demonstrated increased frequencies of central memory (Tcm) subsets (Figures 3B, S3B). Notably, CAR‐T cells with the HVEM CSD showed the highest proportion of T cm cells among the groups (Figure 3B).

(B) Summarized data of CD8+ CAR‐T cell phenotype analysis on day 12 after transduction. (C, D) The CAR‐T cells were cocultured with K562‐Env cells. (C) Summary of IL‐2, IFN‐γ, and TNF‐α in co‐culture experiments of CAR‐T cells with K562‐Env at a T cell to target cell (E/T) ratio of 1 to 10 on Day 3 (n = 3). (D) Summary of frequency of HIVYU2 Envelope+ K562 cells (K.Env) on D3 after coculture with human‐derived CAR‐T cells and Nontransduced (NT) T cells at indicated E/T ratios. Statistical comparisons in Figure D were performed between the D1C‐HM group and each of the following groups individually: pRRL‐GFP, D1C‐28, and D1C‐BB, at indicated E/T ratios.

sec.p: To assess functional activity, CD8⁺ CAR‐T cells were co‐cultured with K562 cells expressing HIV Envelope protein (K.Env). Consistent with previous reports [17, 22], D1C‐HVEM CAR‐T cells secreted significantly higher levels of cytokines, including IL‐2, IFN‐γ, and tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNF‐α), compared to CD28‐ and 4‐1BB‐based CAR‐T cells (Figure 3C). Furthermore, D1C‐HM CAR‐T cells demonstrated superior cytotoxicity against HIV Env⁺ target cells across various E:T ratios (Figure 3D). Elevated cytokine production by D1C‐HM CAR‐T cells was also observed upon stimulation with recombinant gp120 or gp140 protein over D1C‐BB CAR‐T cells (Figure S3C). In addition, neither D1C‐BB nor D1C‐HM CAR‐T cells were activated by Env⁻ K562. HVEM‐based D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells showed elevated activity than CD28‐ and 4‐1BB‐based versions. They demonstrated enhanced, antigen‐specific cytokine production and cytotoxicity against HIV Env⁺ targets.

sec.title: D1C/sCD4 CAR T Cells Show Increased Persistence With Reduced HIV‐1 Infection in NSG‐Hu PBMC Mouse Model
sec.p: The in vivo anti‐HIV activity of sCD4 CAR‐T cells was next evaluated using a human PBMC (hu‐PBMC) mouse model with HIV infection and ART (Figure 4A). To establish the model, irradiated NSG mice were infused with a mixture of uninfected and HIV‐infected human PBMCs, followed by initiation of ART 4 days later. Two weeks after ART initiation, mice were randomized to receive either WT/sCD4 CAR‐T cells or D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells harboring the S85C mutation. Following ART interruption, all groups exhibited viral rebound within 1 week, with no significant differences in the kinetics or magnitude of viremia between all CAR‐T‐treated and control mice (Figure S4A). Interestingly, D1C‐BB CAR‐T cells demonstrated robust persistence during viral rebound, with both CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ CAR‐T cells readily detectable in peripheral blood (Figure 4B,C). Notably, the D1C group exhibited significantly higher levels of circulating CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ CAR‐T cells at day 18 postinfusion. In addition, D1C‐BB CD8⁺ CAR‐T cells were significantly more abundant in the spleens of treated mice at day 18, whereas CD4⁺ CAR‐T cell levels did not reach statistical significance (Figure 4G). These findings indicate that treatment failure was not attributable to insufficient persistence or defective trafficking to lymphoid tissues.

caption.p: D1C/sCD4 CAR T cells show increased persistence with reduced HIV‐1 infection in NSG‐hu PBMC mouse model. (A) Schematic of the in‐vivo study design. Created with BioRender. (B, C) Frequencies of CAR‐T cells among peripheral blood CD4⁺ (B) and CD8⁺ (C) T cells at 1 and 2.5 weeks postinfusion. (D) Frequency of peripheral CD4⁺ T cells at 1 and 2.5 weeks postinfusion. (E) Frequency of splenic CD4⁺ T cells at study endpoint. (F) Percentage of HIV p24⁺ CD8− T cells in spleens. (G) Frequencies of CAR‐T cells among splenic CD8⁺ and CD4⁺ T cells at termination. NT, NonTransduced. P‐values calculated using ordinary one‐way ANOVA Turkeys multiple comparisons test. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001.

sec.p: Importantly, mice treated with D1C‐BB CAR‐T cells exhibited significantly higher percentages of CD4⁺ T cells in the blood (Figure 4D) and in the spleen compared with controls (Figures 4E, S4B), suggesting a protective effect on host CD4⁺ T cell populations. Moreover, the D1C‐BB group showed reduced levels of HIV‐infected CD4⁺ T cells in the spleen (Figures 4F, S4C), indicating that the D1C CAR‐T cells relatively resistant to HIV‐1 infection in lymphoid tissues. These findings demonstrate that D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells conferred partial protection against HIV‐1 infection and improved their persistence in NSG‐hu PBMC mice.

sec.title: D1C/sCD4 CAR T Cells Show Increased Persistence With HIV‐1 Infection In Vivo
sec.p: The in vivo efficacy of HVEM‐based CD4 CAR‐T cells was subsequently assessed in the NSG‐hu HSC humanized mouse model of chronic HIV‐1 infection (Figure 5A). Two weeks after infection was established, mice were infused with 3 × 10⁶ CD8⁺ CAR‐T cells. CAR‐T cell treatment reduced plasma viral load, although no significant difference was observed between the CD4 WT and D1C groups (Figure S5A). Notably, the proportion of p24⁺ CD8− T cells in the spleen was significantly lower in mice treated with D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells compared with those receiving WT/sCD4 CAR‐T cells (Figures 5B, S5B), and a numerically lower frequency of p24⁺ CD8⁺ T cells in D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T treated mice (Figure S5C). One‐week post‐infusion, WT‐HM CAR‐T cells were nearly undetectable in peripheral blood, as detected by myc co‐expression (Figure 5C). In contrast, D1C‐HM CAR‐T cells persisted throughout the 5‐week study. Additionally, mice treated with D1C‐HM CAR‐T cells exhibited a significantly higher number of hCD3+ T cells in the spleen compared to the WT‐HM group (Figure 5D). Moreover, the percentage of myc+ CD8+ CAR‐T cells was significantly higher in the D1C‐HM group in the spleen at termination (Figure 5E). Flow cytometry analysis of spleens from the D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T treated mouse with the highest CAR‐T cell frequency at the endpoint shows that splenic p24⁺ CAR⁺ T cells constitute only ~ 1%, indicating a very low level of infection (Figure S5E). In addition, the frequencies of CD45RO⁺CCR7⁺ and CD45RO⁻CCR7⁺ TCM‐like subsets within the D1C‐HM CAR‐T population were preserved, although reduced relative to preinfusion levels (Figure S5E). Due to their extremely low abundance, it was not feasible to analyze WT/sCD4 CAR‐T cells. The persistence of D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells is likely attributed to resistance to HIV‐1 infection and to cell death. Collectively, these results demonstrate that D1C/sCD4‐based CD8+ CAR‐T cells resist HIV‐1 infection and exhibit protective effects against HIV‐1 pathogenesis in vivo.

sec.title: D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T Cells Show Improved Therapeutic Effect in Controlling HIV‐1 Reservoirs With Reduced HIV‐1 Rebound in Humanized Mice
sec.p: The therapeutic potential of D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells was evaluated in the context of ART‐suppressed HIV infection in vivo. Humanized NSG‐hu HSC mice were infected with HIV‐1, and ART was initiated 6 weeks postinfection. Seven weeks later, the ART‐suppressed mice were divided into groups that received either CD8+ D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells or WT/sCD4 CAR‐T cells. The control group was treated with non‐transduced CD8+ T cells. ART was interrupted 2 days after CAR‐T cell infusion, and the kinetics of HIV rebound were monitored (Figure 6A). HIV rebounded within 2 weeks across all groups following ART interruption, with no significant differences in the initial kinetics or magnitude of viremia between the D1C CAR‐T‐treated mice and other groups during this period (Weeks 13–15). However, by 3 weeks post‐ART removal, the D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cell group showed a marked reduction in the level of viremia compared to control‐treated mice (Figure 6B). Additionally, mice treated with D1C CAR‐T cells displayed a higher percentage of CAR+ cells within the CD8+ T cell population in the spleen compared to the WT CD4 group, with no significant difference observed in the bone marrow (Figure 6C). Notably, the D1C group also exhibited resistance to HIV‐1 infection, with a reduced frequency of HIV‐infected CAR‐T cells in lymphoid tissues in comparison with WT/sCD4 CAR T cells, significantly in the bone marrow (Figure 6D). Taken together, these findings further indicate that the D1C mutation enhances the HIV resistance and survival of D1C/sCD4‐based CAR‐T cells in vivo, leading to improved control over HIV‐1 rebound following ART discontinuation compared to WT/sCD4 CAR‐T cells.

(C) Frequency of CD8 CAR‐T cells in the indicated lymphoid tissues. (D) Relative infection (p24⁺) of CD8 CAR‐T cells in the indicated lymphoid tissues. NT, nontransduced. Symbols represent individual mice; bars/lines show mean ± SEM. P‐ values calculated using ordinary one‐way ANOVA Turkeys multiple comparisons test. *p < 0.05.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: CAR T cell therapy has emerged as a promising strategy in the fight against HIV‐1 [1, 2, 3, 4, 23]. However, the development of CAR‐T cells targeting the HIV envelope (Env) glycoprotein faces significant challenges, primarily due to the susceptibility of these CAR‐T cells to HIV infection and issues related to binding affinity between CAR and HIV Env. Incorporating native CD4 domains into CAR constructs can inadvertently render T cells vulnerable to HIV entry, compromising their therapeutic efficacy. Additionally, achieving optimal binding with HIV Env is crucial to ensure effective targeting and elimination of HIV‐infected cells [24, 25, 26, 27]. To address these challenges, an sCD4‐based CAR containing the S85C mutation within the Ig‐like domain 1 (D1C) was engineered. This mutation facilitates the formation of a disulfide bond between D1C/sCD4 and the HIV Env upon binding, thereby inhibiting the fusion process necessary for viral entry [15, 16]. D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells exhibited elevated T cell activation and cytotoxicity in response to Env stimulation while demonstrating resistance to HIV‐1 infection in vitro and in vivo. In humanized mouse models, D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells demonstrated superior persistence and improved control of HIV rebound following ART interruption compared to wild‐type sCD4 CAR‐T cells.

In vitro studies, 293 T cells expressing the D1C/sCD4 CAR exhibited significantly reduced susceptibility to HIV‐1 infection compared to those expressing WT/sCD4‐based CARs. This resistance was consistent across varying doses of the HIV reporter virus, indicating the robustness of the D1C mutation in conferring protection against HIV‐1. In primary human T cells, CD8+ T cells expressing the D1C/sCD4 CAR were resistant to HIV‐1 infection, suggesting that the D1C mutation effectively reduced susceptibility to HIV‐1 infection in sCD4 CAR‐T cells. These findings underscore the potential of the D1C modification to enhance the durability and safety of CAR‐T cell therapies targeting HIV‐1. This strategic modification renders the CAR‐T cells resistant to HIV infection while preserving their ability to target and eliminate HIV‐infected cells.

Beyond conferring intrinsic resistance to infection, D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells also exhibited elevated antigen‐dependent function against Env⁺ targets. The engineered disulfide “trap” locks HIV Env in a prefusion conformation, prolonging CAR–Env contact and likely improving immunological‐synapse organization and signaling [28]. Accordingly, D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells preserved robust antigen‐specific cytotoxicity and cytokine secretion while remaining nonpermissive to and controlling HIV‐1 infection. These observations are consistent with reports that iterative CARs optimization strengthens T‐cell activation and function [29], as well as with HIV resistance strategies including CCR5 knockout [30], fusion‐inhibitor expression [8], and CD4 truncation [31]. Notably, unlike CCR5 disruption, the D1C modification directly blocks HIV Env‐mediated entry, thereby extending protection to both CCR5‐ and CXCR4‐tropic strains.

In CAR‐T therapy, trogocytosis contributes to antigen loss of target cells and CAR‐T dysfunction [32, 33]. High‐affinity covalent CARs may enhance trogocytosis, leading to impaired CAR‐T function [34, 35]. When trogocytosis was analyzed, the D1C (S85C) mutation did not affect trogocytosis in sCD4‐based CAR‐T cells despite their elevated functional activity. Therefore, the covalent D1C/sCD4–gp120 interaction enhanced CAR‐T cell activity and conferred resistance to HIV‐1 infection, but did not affect the trogocytosis activity compared with WT/sCD4‐based CAR‐T cells. The choice of CSD within CAR constructs plays a pivotal role in determining the efficacy and persistence of CAR‐T cells [36, 37, 38, 39]. Previous analyses have revealed that CAR‐T cells incorporating the HVEM‐derived CSD exhibit superior CAR‐T effector functions compared to those with 4‐1BB or CD28 domains. Consistently, HVEM‐based D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells produced higher levels of key cytokines and demonstrated enhanced cytotoxic activity against HIV Env‐expressing targets. These cells also exhibited a favorable central memory phenotype, characterized by the expression of markers such as CCR7 and CD45RO, which is associated with improved persistence and long‐term efficacy in vivo. These findings further highlight the advantages of HVEM‐derived CSDs in enhancing CAR‐T cell function and persistence in vivo [17, 18, 22].

Studies in humanized mice in vivo further corroborated the enhanced therapeutic potential of D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells. In humanized mice with HIV‐1 infection, treatment with D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cells demonstrated improved persistence compared to CD4 wild‐type CAR‐T cells. This persistence is likely attributed to the resistance of D1C CAR‐T cells to HIV‐1 infection, preventing their depletion. These findings align with previous research indicating that modifications conferring HIV resistance can enhance the durability and efficacy of CAR‐T cell therapies [27]. Moreover, in the context of ART suppression, D1C/sCD4 CAR‐T cell treatment resulted in better control of viral rebound following ART interruption, indicating their potential role in achieving sustained viral remission. Previously engineered CAR‐T cells through different strategies for HIV resistance have demonstrated encouraging results in reducing viral reservoirs and suppressing HIV replication in preclinical studies [30, 40].

In conclusion, the incorporation of the S85C mutation within the CD4 D1 domain of CAR‐T cells effectively addresses major hurdles in HIV Env‐targeting CAR‐T cell therapy by conferring resistance to HIV infection and enhancing sCD4/Env binding with elevated functional activity. The utilization of HVEM‐based CSDs further amplifies these benefits, promoting superior effector functions and persistence in HIV‐infected humanized mice. These findings provide a compelling rationale for the clinical development of D1C‐modified and HVEM‐based sCD4 CAR‐T cells as a durable and effective therapeutic strategy against HIV‐1 infection.

sec.title: Ethics Statement
sec.p: Humanized mouse experiments performed at the University of Maryland, Baltimore (UMB), were approved by the UMB Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) under approval protocol AUP‐00000477. All animal studies were carried out in accordance with recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and purified adult human CD8+ and CD4+ T cells were obtained from de‐identified healthy donors. Human PBMCs were isolated by density gradient centrifugation using Ficoll‐Paque.

sec.title: Hu‐PBMC‐NSG Mouse Model of HIV Infection
sec.p: Human buffy coats were obtained from the Gulf Coast Regional Blood Center (Texas, USA), and PBMCs were isolated by Ficoll‐Paque PLUS (Cytiva) density gradient centrifugation. PBMCs from HIV‐seronegative donors were activated with PHA‐L (3 µg/mL) and cultured in complete RPMI containing recombinant human IL‐2 (100 U/mL). After 3 days, cells were spinoculated with HIV‐1 JRCSF (MOI = 0.1) for 90 min at 1500 × g. Infected PBMCs were cultured until 6%–10% of cells expressed intracellular p24 (typically 4–6 days). 5–7 weeks old NSG mice (Jackson Laboratory) were anesthetized and whole‐body irradiated (2.5 Gy) before intraperitoneal injection of 1 × 10⁷ infected PBMCs. Mice were allowed to engraft for 4 days before initiating ART via medicated chow for 17 days. ART was discontinued immediately before adoptive transfer of CAR‐T cells (5 × 10⁶ total T cells; E:T ratio = 1:2). At necropsy (2.5 weeks posttransfer), spleen and other tissues were collected for analysis of CAR‐T cell persistence and viral parameters.

sec.title: Construction of Humanized Mice
sec.p: Human fetal liver tissues were obtained from elective or medically indicated termination of pregnancy through a nonprofit intermediary working with outpatient clinics (Advanced Bioscience Resources). Approval for animal work was obtained from the UMB, IACUC. We constructed CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) transplanted humanized NSG (NOD‐scid IL2rgnull) mice (hu‐NSG) through intra‐liver injection of 2 × 105 purified HSC individually as previously reported [41]. Human immune cell engraftment was detected by flow cytometry 12 weeks after transplantation.

sec.title: Virus and Infection
sec.p: HIV‐1JR‐CSF was generated by transfection of 293 T cells using the calcium phosphate method. Plasmids were obtained from the NIH AIDS Reagent Program. Virus titer was measured by either p24 ELISA (CELL BIOLABS) or MAGI‐CCR5 [42, 43]. Animals were infected with HIV‐1JR‐CSF at a dose of 5 ng p24/mouse, through retro‐orbital injection.

sec.title: Combination ART
sec.p: Individual tablets of TRUVADA (tenofovir/emtricitabine; Gilead Sciences) or raltegravir (Merck) were crushed into fine powder and manufactured as 5BXL by TestDiet based on previously published [44].

sec.title: HIV Viral Load Quantitation
sec.p: Viral RNA was isolated from plasma (20 μL) using the QiaAmp viral RNA mini kit (QIAGEN). Viral loads were determined using quantitative reverse transcription‐polymerase chain reaction using TaqMan® Fast Virus 1‐Step PCR kit (ThermoFisher Scientific) and QuantStudio 6 Flex PCR system (Applied Biosystems) (detection limit ≈ 400 copies/mL) [41, 44].

sec.title: Plasmid Construction
sec.p: The amino acid sequences for the HIV‐specific CD4‐based CAR constructs the CD4‐derived variant specific for HIV, linked to a co‐expressed myc, a CD8 hinge and TM domain, followed by a following intracellular domain: CD28/CD3‐z, 4‐1BB/CD3‐z, and HVEM/CD3‐z. In this study, each CAR is artificially synthesized by GenScript. To make the various CD4‐CAR‐expressing lentiviral vectors, the NdeI/MluI‐digested each CD4 derived DNA fragment and each of the MluI/SalI‐digested CSSD DNA fragments were ligated into NdeI/SalI‐digested pRRL backbone plasmid.

sec.title: Lentivirus Production and Transfection
sec.p: Lentivirus particles were generated using lentiviral vector plasmid with the psPAX2/pMD2.G packaging system. The plasmids were transfected into HEK293T cells using Lipofectamine 3000 (Life Technologies), according to the manufacturer's instructions. Transfected HEK293T cell supernatant was collected 48 and 72 h after transfection, filtered through a sterile 0.45‐mm nylon syringe‐driven filter, and concentrated by ultracentrifugation at 25 000 rpm for 2.5 h at 4 C or using Lenti‐X concentrator (Takara). Supernatant was aspirated and the virus pellet was resuspended in 500 µL total volume and stored at −80 C. The lentiviral titers were measured on Jurkat cells based on the percentage of co‐expressed myc by flow cytometry.

sec.title: Luciferase Reporter Assay
sec.p: Engineered 293 T cells or primary T cells were spinoculated with HIV‐Luc pseudoviruses at 1200 × g for 2 h at room temperature in the presence of 8 µg/mL Polybrene (Sigma‐Aldrich). After spin infection, cells were washed and cultured for 72 h before analysis. Infection efficiency was assessed by measuring luciferase activity using the Pierce™ Gaussia Luciferase Glow Assay Kit (Thermo Scientific, Cat# 16161) on a microplate luminometer.

sec.title: Cell Lines and Culture
sec.p: The culture media, minimum essential medium (MEM), DMEM, and RPMI (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA), were both supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 2 mM glutamine (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 10 U/mL penicillin, and 10 mg/mL streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific). HEK293T cells were cultured in DMEM, and Jurkat cells were maintained in RPMI. K562 and K562‐Env cells were also cultured with RPMI medium. T/CAR‐T cells (described below) were cultured in RPMI medium supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin/streptomycin, and 200 IU/mL recombinant human IL‐2 (PeproTech). Cells were incubated at 37 C in a 5% CO2 humidified atmosphere. All cell lines were used within 20 passages of thawing. Cell line authentication and Mycoplasma testing were performed by the vendor and not reevaluated throughout the course of the studies.

sec.title: CAR T‐Cell Preparation
sec.p: Human PBMCs from healthy donors were prepared by Ficoll‐Paque Plus (Cytiva) density gradient. Cells were cryopreserved at a density of 20–30 million cells/mL in 90% FBS/10% dimethyl sulfoxide and stored in liquid nitrogen for CAR T‐cell preparation. To manufacture CAR T cells, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from thawed PBMCs were purified by negative selection using MojoSort Human CD4+ or CD8+ enrichment cocktails (BioLegend) according to the manufacturer's instructions. All T cells were cultured at 1e6 cells/mL in complete RPMI supplemented with 200 U/mL human IL‐2 (PeproTech). T cells were stimulated with anti‐CD3/CD28 Dynabeads(Life Technologies) at a 1:1bead‐to cell ratio at 37 C, 5% CO2% and 95% humidity incubation conditions. Roughly 24 h after stimulation, half of the medium was removed and replaced with 200–300 µL of concentrated lentivirus supernatant for CAR transduction at a multiplicity of infection round 5. On Day 5, the Dynabeads were removed from cell culture by magnetic separation. Expansion medium was changed every other day throughout cell culture spanning 8–10 days, or as necessary to adjust cell concentration to 0.5e6 cells/mL, and then the cells were used for experiments in vitro or in vivo experiments.

sec.title: Co‐Culture Assay
sec.p: To determine cytotoxicity of the CAR‐T cells, target cells (5e4) were seeded in each well of a 96‐well flat‐bottom plate. The CAR‐T cells were added at different effector‐to‐target ratios (see also in the figure legend). On Day 3, the culture supernatants, including cells, were harvested and centrifuged to separate cells and cell‐free supernatants. The remaining target cells were determined as CD3‐ cells by flow cytometry. Collected supernatants were used to determine IL‐2, TNF‐α, and IFN‐γ secretion using human IL‐2, TNF‐α, and IFN‐γ ELISA MAX Deluxe (all from BioLegend), according to the manufacturer's instructions. In cases of unequal percentages of CAR‐transduced cells in the cultures, untransduced T cells were added to ensure that both the number of CAR+ T cells and the total number of T cells remained consistent across the CAR‐T cell groups.

sec.title: Ag‐Specific Stimulation of CAR‐T Cells
sec.p: Different CD4‐based CAR T cells (5e5 per well) were seeded into plates pre‐coated with recombinant HIV‐1 gp120/gp140 (4 µg/well) and incubated for 24 h at 37°C in a humidified incubator. Following stimulation, culture supernatants were harvested for ELISA‐based quantification of activation‐associated cytokines (IL‐2 and IFN‐γ) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Cells were then washed and stained for surface markers for flow‐cytometric analysis.

sec.title: FACS‐Based Trogocytosis Assay
sec.p: K562‐WT and K562‐Env target cells were labeled with PKH26 according to the manufacturer's instructions (Sigma‐Aldrich). Immediately following staining, PKH26‐labeled target cells were co‐cultured with CAR‐Jurkat cells (3 × 10⁵) per well in 96‐well plates, using target‐to‐effector ratios of 1:1, 2:1, or 4:1. 6 h post‐co‐culture at 37°C and 5% CO2, cells were washed twice with PBS and stained with F c blocker and Fixable Aqua Stain (Thermofisher Scientific) in 50 µL of PBS for 30 min at 4°C. Cells were washed and stained with cMyc‐biotin in 50 µL of PBS for 30 min at 4°C followed by secondary staining using an anti‐biotin antibody in 50 µL of PBS for 30 min at 4°C. After staining, cells were resuspended in fixing buffer (2.5% paraformaldehyde) and analyzed by Fluorescence‐Activated Cell Sorting (FACS). Trogocytosis was measured by the acquisition of PKH26 dye by CAR+ (cMyc) cells from stained CAR‐ target cells.

sec.title: ELISA
sec.p: Human CAR T cells were cocultured with target cells for 72 h or gp120/gp140 for 24 h at the indicated E:T ratios. Media from the cocultured wells were collected after centrifugation removal of cell debris. Supernatants were diluted into 3 to 10 times before detection. Cytokines in supernatants were measured using human ELISA kits (BioLegend), IL‐2, TNF‐α, and IFN‐γ, respectively. The detection was performed according to the manufacturer's instructions, and the absorbance was detected by GloMax (Promega). Standard curves were illustrated by standards provided by kits. Concentration of cytokines were calculated by multiply dilution ratios.

sec.title: Flow Cytometry
sec.p: Antibodies used in flow cytometry were obtained from BioLegend otherwise indicated. CAR expressions on the transduced Jurkat E6.1 cells or primary T cells were analyzed with anti‐c‐myc tag antibody (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX), followed by anti‐mouse immunogloburins (Igs)‐ PE antibody (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA). Surface staining was performed in PBS containing 2% fetal calf serum and 2 mM EDTA using anti‐human antibodies from BioLegend: CD45 (2D1), CD3 (OKT3), CD4 (OKT4), CD8 (RPA‐T8), PD‐1 (EH12.2H7), CD45RO (UCHL1), CCR7 (G043H7), and CD95(DX2). Intracellular proteins were stained for with a cell fixation and cell permeabilization kit (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer's instructions using antibodies from the following sources: Beckman Coulter: HIV‐1 core antigen (KC57). Flow cytometry data were acquired on a FACS Canto II cell analyzer (Becton‐Dickinson) and analyzed using FlowJo V10.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism software (version 9.4.1; GraphPad, San Diego, CA, USA), while flow cytometry data were analyzed using FlowJo software (version 10.8.1; FlowJo, Ashland, OR, USA). Results are presented as means with error bars representing SEM. Mean comparisons were performed using one‐way ANOVA, or two‐way ANOVA or paired/unpaired t‐tests, with Welch's correction applied when appropriate. For data presented on a logarithmic scale, nonparametric tests were employed. Hypotheses regarding fold changes were tested against a mean of 1. All p‐values were two‐tailed, with statistical significance established at p < 0.05.
